extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (or beginning graduate) mathematics students studying metric spaces, topology, and real analysis (Rudin-style exercises)
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and prove a list of exercises about metric spaces, compactness, connectedness, separability, subsequences, Cauchy sequences, and related topology/analysis topics; many items demand constructions, counterexamples, or use of earlier Rudin results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show that d_n is a metric on Z
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that the function d_n defined on Z (using the largest exponent a such that an integer is divisible by n^a) satisfies the metric axioms; in particular prove the ultrametric inequality (c') dn(p,q) ≤ max(dn(p,r), dn(r,q)) and deduce the usual triangle inequality (c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let e_n(s) be the largest integer a such that s is divisible by n^a (take it 0 when appropriate). Note: when n is prime p, this yields the p-adic metric on Z. Emphasize verifying (c') (the ultrametric inequality), which is stronger than the usual triangle inequality; mention that the ultrametric property fails in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated limit sets (existence for prescribed finite depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each positive integer n, construct a subset E of some metric space X such that L^{n-1}(E) ≠ ∅ but L^n(E) = ∅ (where L denotes the limit-point operator and L^k denotes k-fold iteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may use X = R or another metric space. The exercise asks an explicit construction producing exactly n–1 nonempty iterated limit sets before emptiness occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit points in terms of closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a metric space, E ⊆ X, and p ∈ X. Show that p is a limit point of E if and only if p ∈ cl(E) − {p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definition of closure and limit point; this is a basic equivalence connecting limit points and closures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed balls equal {q : d(p,q) ≤ r} and examples of inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a point p and r>0 define V_r(p) and show V_r(p) is closed and equals {q ∈ X : d(p,q) ≤ r}. Then give four examples (choices of metric space X, point p, and r) to exhibit all four possible combinations of equality/inequality among the three sets: N_r(p) ⊆ N_r(p) ⊆ V_r(p) (displayed in the text — interpret as various open/closed-radius neighborhood variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a): prove the closedness and the characterization. Part (b): produce an example where all three sets equal; an example where the first inclusion is equality but second not; where second is equality but first not; and where all three are distinct. Pay attention to whether the metric is discrete, discrete-like, or continuous (R will provide standard examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite metric space that does not embed isometrically into any R^k
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X = {w,x,y,z} with d(w,others)=1 and d between any two of {x,y,z} equal to 2. (a) Verify this defines a metric. (b) Show no map f : X → R^k preserves all distances. (c) Investigate if there exists a 5-point metric space every 4-point subset of which embeds isometrically into some R^k but the whole 5-point space does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) is checking metric axioms. Part (b) requires using properties of Euclidean distances (e.g., triangle inequalities in Euclidean space) to derive a contradiction. Part (c) asks for a further construction or example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite metric space has uncountably many open sets
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Prove any infinite metric space X contains a countable family of pairwise disjoint neighborhoods (i.e., points p_i with radii r_i such that N_{r_i}(p_i) are pairwise disjoint). (b) Deduce X has uncountably many open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful with spaces like {1/n} ∪ {0} ⊆ R: you cannot take any p_i equal to 0 in that construction. Suggested step: given any infinite subset E ⊆ X and two distinct points x,y ∈ X, show at least one of x,y has a neighborhood missing infinitely many points of E. Use shrinking radii to avoid closures capturing infinitely many points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated interior and closure operations (at most 7 distinct sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how many distinct sets can be obtained from a subset E of X by repeatedly applying closure and interior operators in succession. Prove identities like (E°)° = E° and cl(int(cl(int(E)))) = cl(int(E)), then deduce one can get at most 7 distinct sets (including E). Exhibit an example E ⊆ R that attains 7 distinct sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints suggest using standard identities (Theorem 2.2.7 and Rudin results) and observing that repeated application of the same operator twice has no extra effect. Keep track of operator order; cl and int alternation suffices. Provide an explicit R example for sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated closures and complements (at most 14 distinct sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show E° can be obtained by closures and complements. (b) Deduce that any set obtainable by closure and interior is also obtainable by closure and complement. (c) Deduce at most 14 distinct sets can be obtained by closure and complement operations starting from E. (e) Give an example E ⊆ R that yields 14 distinct sets. (f) Ask whether there exists a nonempty metric space X and subset E such that a set obtained using closure plus an even number of complements equals one obtained with an odd number of complements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use previous exercise 2.2:20 and Rudin's results. For (f) provide proof or counterexample as requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative closures and interiors: truth of implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Given X metric, Y ⊆ X, and E, F ⊆ Y, determine which of the following hold in general: (a) cl_Y(E) = cl_Y(F) ⇒ cl_X(E) = cl_X(F). (b) cl_X(E) = cl_X(F) ⇒ cl_Y(E) = cl_Y(F). (c) int_Y(E) = int_Y(F) ⇒ int_X(E) = int_X(F). (d) int_X(E) = int_X(F) ⇒ int_Y(E) = int_Y(F). Provide proofs when true and counterexamples when false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hint suggests constructing the right-hand sets from the left-hand ones in a way independent of E or F for the true cases; find explicit counterexamples when false.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False exercises about open coverings of [−10,10]
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide true/false for a list of statements about open coverings of [−10,10] by intervals (examples with shifted radii and discrete subcollections) and about compactness: (d) If some open covering of K has a finite subcover, then K is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are straightforward verification or counterexample tasks; pay attention to precise quantifiers and whether a given subcollection indeed covers the set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of finitely many compact sets is compact
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that if E1, ..., En are compact subsets of a metric space X, then their union E1 ∪ ... ∪ En is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard finite-subcover argument: given an open cover of the union, restrict to each compact Ei to get finite subcovers, then take their union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering a compact set by neighborhoods with limited overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be compact and ε>0. Show there exists a subset S ⊆ X such that the sets N_ε(s) (s∈S) cover X and the distance between any two distinct points of S is ≥ ε/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approach: first find finite T so that N_{ε/2}(t) cover X. Then select a maximal subset S ⊆ T with pairwise distances ≥ ε/2. Show the N_ε(s) cover X. Remark: with Choice/Zorn one can do this in general spaces without compactness; here compactness ensures S finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packing points into a compact set forces closeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose K is compact and ε>0. Show there exists N such that every N-point subset of K contains two points at distance < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: cover K by finitely many ε/2-neighborhoods; choose N greater than the number of these sets so by pigeonhole principle some neighborhood contains at least two points whose distance is < ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of essential indices characterizes compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Define for a cover {G_α} of X an index β to be essential if removing G_β leaves the collection no longer a cover. Show X is compact iff every open cover has only finitely many essential indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the hard direction, if X is not compact use 2:R26 to get a countable set without limit points and verify that removing any single set leaves a noncover. A proof avoiding 2:R26 would be interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant coverings of compact sets admit finite redundant subcover
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K be compact and {G_α} a cover such that every point of K belongs to at least two sets of the cover. Show there exists a finite subcover in which every point of K still belongs to at least two sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compactness and a finite-subcover selection argument, while maintaining the redundancy property by choosing sets appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: R (the real line) is closed in any metric space that contains it as a subspace
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a metric space containing R as a subspace (with induced metric equal to |r−s|), prove R is closed in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: points close to each other in R belong to a compact subset; use compactness arguments to show limit points of R lie in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False: perfect sets and Cantor set
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the statements are true: (a) If E is perfect and F is closed subset of E then F is perfect. (b) The Cantor set is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are conceptual checks: supply proofs or counterexamples. (Answers later in text indicate both are false.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit construction proving Theorem 2.43 (uncountability of perfect sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an explicit nested neighborhood construction (binary splitting of neighborhoods with closures contained appropriately) to obtain uncountably many distinct points in P as per Theorem 2.43, rather than using contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each step split a neighborhood into two disjoint neighborhoods each meeting P, refine further, and show chains of nested neighborhoods produce distinct points; optionally shrink radii to make intersections singletons to obtain a perfect subset homeomorphic in cardinality to Cantor set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect compact sets are uncountable (generalized Theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if E is nonempty, perfect, and compact in any metric space X, then E is uncountable. Then deduce Theorem 2.43 in R^k using compactness arguments and earlier results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to adapt the binary-splitting proof; note that part (a) requires compactness of E, so slightly different from the Euclidean theorem which uses other theorems as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two metrics on the Cantor set: ultrametric and Euclidean give same topology
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Define t(p,q) to be the largest n at which p,q are together at the nth stage of the Cantor construction, set d(p,q)=2^{-t(p,q)} (0 if p=q), and show d is a metric satisfying the ultrametric inequality. (b) Show the open sets with respect to d are the same as those from the standard |x−y| metric from R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) shows ultrametric property. Part (b) shows the two metrics induce the same topology on the Cantor set — use structure of intervals in the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of connected sets
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Prove a subset E of a metric space is connected iff the only subsets of E that are both open and closed in the relative topology are E and ∅. (b) Deduce equivalent formulations for closed and open subsets of metric spaces in terms of unions of disjoint closed/open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard characterization — prove both directions and derive corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set with enough connected subsets is connected
rubrics_metrics.description: Show E ⊆ X is connected iff for every pair p,q ∈ E there exists a connected subset A ⊆ E containing both p and q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the idea that connectivity is 'path-connectedness' in a broader sense: if any two points can be joined inside by a connected set then the whole set cannot be separated into disjoint open pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a union of sets is connected
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Suppose A and B are connected nonempty subsets. Show A ∪ B is connected iff A and B are not separated (i.e., their closures meet or intersect appropriately). (b) If A and B are both disconnected, can their union be connected? Provide examples/analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) is standard; part (b) invites counterexamples where pieces interlock to yield a connected union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultrametric spaces are totally disconnected (cannot be connected when more than one point)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Prove ultrametric inequality is equivalent to: for any three points p,q,r, at least two of d(p,q), d(q,r), d(r,p) are equal and the third ≤ that common value. (b) Show a metric space with more than one point satisfying this inequality cannot be connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the property to find disjoint nonempty clopen sets splitting the space. Apply to Cantor-set metric to deduce no subset with more than one point is connected in that ultrametric; use topological invariance to infer same about subsets as subsets of R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectedness criterion for compact spaces via positive separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Show a compact metric space X is connected iff it cannot be written as X = A ∪ B with inf_{a∈A,b∈B} d(a,b) > 0. Prove one direction for arbitrary metric spaces and the other direction uses compactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a positive infimum exists, the two sets are separated by neighborhoods; use compactness to reverse implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable basis property implies separability
rubrics_metrics.description: Show every metric space with a countable basis is separable (i.e., has a countable dense subset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: choose one point from each member of the basis to produce a countable dense subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separability inherited by subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Show every subset E of a separable metric space X is separable as a metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If S is a countable dense subset of X, choose an at-most-countable subset T of E approximating points of E; alternatives rely on 2.6:1 or using standard density arguments. The exercise suggests multiple approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False questions on sequences and convergence (3.1:0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide truth of various statements about sequences: e.g., a sequence in E that converges in X converges in E; properties of sums and boundedness of convergent sequences; limit inequalities when a sequence is bounded above by constant c, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle each item separately; the text provides final answer keys for many True/False items elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent sequence plus its limit forms a compact set
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If a sequence (p_i) in X converges to p then the set {p} ∪ {p_i : i=1,2,...} is compact. (b) Deduce that a subset S ⊆ X is closed iff for every compact E ⊆ X, the intersection S ∩ E is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) uses sequential compactness arguments in metric spaces; part (b) is a corollary leveraging compactness properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse to Theorem 3.6(a): sequential compactness implies compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce (from 2:R26 or otherwise) that if every sequence in X has a convergent subsequence, then X is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard equivalence of sequential compactness and compactness in metric spaces; the exercise suggests using earlier results (2:R26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct sequences in R with prescribed subsequential limit sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Find explicit sequences in R whose sets of subsequential limit points are: (a) empty set, (b) the integers, (c) [0,1], and (d) all of R. Provide constructions and proofs of the asserted limit sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may give explicit sequences or describe constructions (e.g., enumerations, interleaving, scaled dense sequences). Prove properties rigorously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequential limit set of product sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (s_n) and (t_n) be bounded real sequences with subsequential limit sets E and F respectively. Show the subsequential limit set of (s_n t_n) is contained in E·F = {e f : e∈E, f∈F}. Discuss cases where inclusion is proper or fails if boundedness is dropped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) is a containment proof; (b) produce examples demonstrating strict inclusion; (c) show necessity of boundedness. Later parts ask versions for R^k and absolute values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequential limits of unions of sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If a sequence (a_k) is union of two subsequences with sets of subsequential limits E1 and E2, show E = E1 ∪ E2. (b) Generalize to finite unions: lim sup equals max of lim sups. (c) Show infinite unions can behave differently; construct decompositions into countably many subsequences converging to any given point of E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions and elementary subsequence selection arguments; part (c) suggests constructing disjoint subsequences approaching any given subsequential limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of subsequential limit sets (3.2:6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence (s_n) in metric space X with subsequential limit set E, prove various properties: (a) when X=R then E is closed; (b) for every ε>0, all but finitely many n have d(s_n, E) < ε; (c) if X is compact then E is connected; (d) give example in R^2 where E is not connected; (e) in R^k if E not connected then it contains an unbounded connected subset; (f) if X=R^k and (s_n) not convergent then E is perfect; (g) existence of sequences whose subsequential limit set is entire connected compact X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each part separately; use compactness, connectivity, and construction of examples (esp. for (d),(e),(g)). For (f) use that limit points of subsequences are accumulation points.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False on Cauchy sequences (3.3:0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide truth of statements: (a) any Cauchy sequence in X that converges in X is Cauchy in E; (b) every convergent sequence is Cauchy; (c) every subset of R^k that is complete as a metric space is bounded, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary verifications; some require counterexamples in particular metric spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subsets and completeness relations (3.3:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If Y ⊆ X is complete as a metric space then Y is closed in X. (b) If X is complete and Y closed in X then Y is complete. (c) If Y is such that in every metric space X containing Y, Y is closed in X, then Y is complete. Prove each part (they are related but independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) and (b) are standard. Part (c) suggests contrapositive proof: if Y is not complete produce an X containing Y where Y is not closed by adjoining a limit point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete bounded (connected) metric spaces need not be compact
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show the metric space from 2:R10 is bounded and complete but not compact. (b) Give an example of a connected metric space that is bounded, complete, but not compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct counterexamples, e.g., complete non-compact spaces; examples often use sequences with no convergent subsequence but completeness maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential tests for Cauchy sequences (3.3:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show by example the condition lim_{n→∞} d(s_n, s_{n+1}) = 0 does not imply the sequence is Cauchy in general, and conversely. (b) Investigate whether there exists a sequence of index-pairs ((m_k,n_k)) such that for every sequence (s_n) the condition lim_k d(s_{m_k}, s_{n_k}) = 0 is equivalent to (s_n) being Cauchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) wants explicit counterexamples where adjacent differences vanish but sequence not Cauchy. Part (b) suggests exploring properties of index-pair sequences and constructing positive/negative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse to Theorem 3.6(a) via continuous function f and open cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Given X in which every sequence has a convergent subsequence, prove X is compact by (a) defining f(x) = sup{ε ≤ 1 : some member of cover contains N_ε(x)} and showing f is continuous and positive-valued, (b) deducing inf_x f(x) > 0 and constructing a finite subcover using balls of radius c < inf f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the outlined construction: assume contrary that inf f(x)=0, produce sequence x_n with f(x_n)→0, obtain contradiction using convergent subsequence. Then pick c>0 and greedily select centers with balls of radius c whose chosen covering members produce a finite subcover by compactness argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper and lower limits (reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Section 3.4 on upper and lower limits of sequences; relevant Rudin exercises include computing limsup/liminf and properties of limsup of sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a header pointing to subsequent exercises (3:R4, 3:R5) not fully expanded in this chunk.
